title: Query vs. Update Methods
section: 38. Build Your First Defi (Decentralised Finance) DApp - DBANK
summary: Explains why calls that change canister state take seconds (update calls go through consensus) while read-only query calls return in milliseconds. Adds a public query function checkBalance with an async return type.

concepts.heading: Update vs query calls
points: topUp and withdraw modify a variable, so they are update methods: the change must be written to the blockchain and agreed by the network, which takes around 2-3 seconds in the demo (2.14 s measured).
A query method only reads state and changes nothing, so it skips consensus and answers in milliseconds (0.014 s measured in Candid UI).
Rule of thumb: if the function does not change state, make it a query; reserve update calls for real writes. Important for responsive apps and games.
By default a public func is an update method; the query modifier opts into the fast read path.

concepts.heading: Declaring a query function
points: Syntax: `public query func checkBalance() : async Nat { ... };` The query keyword goes between public and func.
Return type is declared after a colon following the parameter list.

Shared (public) functions that return a value must have an async return type, so the type is written `async Nat` rather than plain Nat; otherwise the compiler complains that a shared query function needs an async syntactic return type.

Declarations inside an actor are separated by semicolons. A missing semicolon after the previous function causes an error. The final one can technically omit it, but adding it everywhere keeps things consistent.

concepts.heading: Sync vs async (concept)
points: Synchronous work runs one step at a time, each step blocking the next, like a single track; asynchronous work lets tasks proceed independently and finish in any order.
Web analogy: a modern page fires many requests at once and renders resources as they arrive, so slow ones don't block fast ones or user interaction.
Canister results come back asynchronously, which is why the async keyword shows up in return types.

concepts.heading: Seeing it in Candid UI
points: After redeploy and refreshing Candid UI, checkBalance shows a Query button (update functions show Call). Clicking it returns the balance immediately with a timing readout.
Comparing this with clicking Call on topUp or withdraw shows the latency gap directly.

task.starting_point: DBank with public topUP and withdraw update functions.
task.goal: Expose a fast read-only balance getter and observe the speed difference.
steps: Add `public query func checkBalance() : async Nat` returning currentValue.
Make sure the previous function ends with a semicolon.
Run dfx deploy, refresh Candid UI, press Query on checkBalance and note the time.
Press Call on topUp or withdraw and compare.
task.expected_result: Query returns in a few hundredths of a second; update calls take roughly 2-3 seconds.

pitfalls: Omitting async in the return type of a public function.
Using a query method to change state (changes are not persisted).
(Extra) Local replica timings are far shorter than a mainnet round trip would be for updates; treat figures as illustrative.
